title: Foundation Pack 002 — River and Bridge
description: A beginner multilingual semantic language pack about river, bridge, crossing, water and boat. It teaches prepositions, location markers, Japanese particles and basic sentence building.

grammarExplanation: A single noun names a thing or place.
A bridge helps people cross from one side to another.
German nouns are capitalised.
'Brücke' is feminine, so 'the bridge' is 'die Brücke'.
'pont' means bridge.
French normally adds an article in a noun phrase.
'puente' means bridge.
Spanish normally adds an article in a noun phrase.
Chinese does not need an article like 'a' or 'the' here.
'橋' means bridge.
Japanese does not use articles like 'a' or 'the'.
'橋' means bridge.
'the' points to a specific bridge.
English commonly uses articles before singular nouns.
'die' is the feminine definite article.
German articles depend on noun gender and case.
'le' is the masculine definite article.
French nouns usually need articles.
'el' is the masculine definite article.
Spanish nouns usually need articles.
Chinese often does not translate 'the' directly.
The noun alone can mean 'the bridge' when context is clear.
Japanese has no article equivalent to 'the'.
The noun alone can mean 'the bridge' in context.
'across' shows movement from one side to the other.
'the bridge' is the route or path.

tokens.meaning: from one side to the other

grammarExplanation: 'über' can mean over/across.
With movement across something, German uses the accusative after 'über'.
French commonly says 'sur le pont' for being on/across the bridge.
'le pont' means 'the bridge'.
'por' can show route or movement across a place.
'el puente' means 'the bridge'.
Chinese uses '過' before the object to mean cross/go across.
No article is needed.
'を' marks the thing being crossed.
'渡って' is a connecting form of 'cross'.

tokens.grammarNote: The particle を marks the bridge as what is crossed.

grammarExplanation: 'cross' is the action.
'the bridge' is what is crossed.
In an infinitive phrase, German can place the object before the infinitive verb.
'überqueren' means 'to cross'.
'traverser' means 'to cross'.
The object follows the verb.
'cruzar' means 'to cross'.
The object follows the verb.
Chinese keeps a simple verb + object order.
'過橋' means cross the bridge.
Japanese usually places the verb at the end.
'橋を' means the bridge is what is crossed.

tokens.grammarNote: Japanese verbs usually come at the end.

grammarExplanation: 'We' is the subject.
'cross' is the action.
'the bridge' is the object or route.
In a simple German main clause, the conjugated verb is in second position.
'überqueren' comes after 'Wir'.
'Nous' is the subject.
'traversons' is the conjugated verb for 'we cross'.
Spanish can omit the subject pronoun because the verb ending shows 'we'.
'Cruzamos' means 'we cross'.
Chinese follows a direct Subject + Verb + Object order.
No article like 'the' is needed.

ja.text: 私たちは橋を渡ります。

grammarExplanation: '私たちは' marks 'we' as the topic.
'橋を' marks the bridge as the object/route.
Japanese verbs usually come at the end.

'bateau' means boat.
It uses the masculine article 'le'.
'barco' means boat.
It uses the masculine article 'el'.
Chinese does not need an article here.
'船' means boat/ship.
Japanese does not use articles like 'a' or 'the'.
'船' means boat/ship.
'the' points to a specific boat.
'das' is the neuter definite article.
'Boot' is a neuter noun.
'le' is the masculine definite article.

Chinese often does not translate 'the' directly.

'on' shows the boat is on the surface of the river.

'auf' means on.
'dem' is the dative form of 'der' after a location preposition.

'la rivière' means the river.
Spanish often uses 'en' for in/on/at depending on context.
'el río' means the river.
'在...上' means on/at something.
The place comes between 在 and 上.
'の上' means 'on top of / on'.
'に' marks location.
